title: Imperial Pilsner Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What an imperial pilsner is, how it differs from a classic Czech or German pilsner and why it is so hard to brew well.
teaser: A pilsner turned up to 8% ABV with the bitterness to match. Here is what happens when you supersize a classic.
standfirst: Imperial pilsner takes the cleanest, most delicate beer style in the world and makes it big. Done well, it is a strong, crisp, bitter lager with nowhere to hide. Here is what defines it and how to taste one.
sections:
The original pilsner was first brewed in Plzeň, in what is now the Czech Republic, in 1842. It is pale, crisp and bitter, usually around 4.5 to 5.5% ABV. German brewers adapted it into a drier, lighter-bodied version. Both are covered in our pilsner style guide.

Imperial pilsner is a modern craft idea. Brewers take the pilsner recipe and scale everything up: more malt, more hops, more alcohol. The word imperial is borrowed from imperial stout and imperial IPA, where it has come to mean stronger. Our guide to imperial and double in beer names explains how that habit started.
What the numbers usually look like

There is no single official definition, so versions vary. Most imperial pilsners land somewhere around 7 to 9% ABV. Bitterness is high, often 50 IBU or more, enough to balance the extra malt. Colour stays pale gold to deep gold, a little darker than a standard pilsner because the bigger grist carries more colour.

Competitions handle it differently. Some judges see it as a strong pale lager, others as an experimental or specialty beer. That ambiguity is part of the style's character. It sits between a lager and an IPA, borrowing the crispness of one and the hop intensity of the other.
Why strong lager is hard to brew

Lager yeast likes cool fermentation, usually around 8 to 13 °C. At higher alcohol it works under more stress. Stressed yeast can leave behind sulphur, diacetyl or acetaldehyde, flavours that a clean pilsner cannot hide. Brewers pitch more yeast than usual, oxygenate well and give the beer extra time.

Lagering takes longer too. A standard pilsner might spend a few weeks cold conditioning. An imperial version often needs considerably longer for the yeast to clean up and the flavours to settle. That tank time costs money, which is one reason these beers are rare and usually priced above standard lager.

Water plays its part. The soft water of Plzeň is famous for letting hop bitterness come through smoothly. Hard, high-bicarbonate water makes heavy bitterness feel coarse. Brewers with hard borewell supplies often treat or dilute their water before brewing any strong, very bitter pale lager.
The hops do the heavy lifting

A classic Czech pilsner uses Saaz hops for a soft, spicy, herbal character. German versions often use Hallertau, Tettnang or Spalt. Imperial pilsners may stick with these traditional varieties in large amounts, or swap in American and New Zealand hops for citrus and tropical notes.

That choice divides the style in two. Brewers using noble hops make a strong, very bitter, herbal lager that tastes like a magnified pilsner. Brewers using new world hops make something closer to an India pale lager. Both are valid. Read the label or ask the bar which kind you are getting.

Pour it into a tall, narrow glass and look for brilliant clarity and a dense white head. The aroma should be dominated by hops, with clean bready malt underneath. On the palate expect a firm, lasting bitterness, a fuller body than a regular pilsner and a dry finish.

The alcohol should be present but warming rather than hot. If it tastes of nail polish or harsh spirit, the fermentation ran too warm. A buttery slickness means diacetyl that the yeast did not clean up. A cooked corn smell points to DMS, often from a weak boil. These faults are far easier to spot in a pale lager than in a dark or hazy beer.

India already drinks a lot of strong lager, usually built for strength and price rather than hop flavour. An imperial pilsner is a very different proposition: full malt, real hop bitterness and a clean, long fermentation. Side by side, the two show how much brewing choices shape a beer at the same alcohol level.

Treat it with respect in the heat. At 8% ABV a large glass on a hot afternoon is a lot of alcohol. Serve it around 6 to 8 °C in a smaller glass, drink water alongside and never drive afterwards. It goes well with spiced grilled food, where its bitterness cuts through fat and chilli.
Training your palate on clean beer

Pale lagers are the hardest beers to judge because every fault stands out and every subtlety matters. Telling clean malt sweetness from DMS or noting the line between firm bitterness and harshness takes practice with known samples. That is exactly the kind of structured tasting a sensory course provides and a beer shelf cannot.

For a first step, pour a standard pilsner and an imperial pilsner side by side. Taste the standard one first. Note what changes in bitterness, body, alcohol warmth and hop aroma when the same idea is scaled up.
faqs: How strong is an imperial pilsner?
Most are around 7 to 9% ABV, well above the 4.5 to 5.5% of a classic pilsner.
Yes. It is fermented with lager yeast at cool temperatures and given extended cold conditioning.
What is the difference between imperial pilsner and India pale lager?
There is overlap. Imperial pilsners with traditional European hops taste like a magnified pilsner, while those with new world hops drift towards India pale lager.
Strong lagers need more yeast, careful fermentation and long lagering, which ties up tanks and makes them expensive to produce.
